clue.text: He just appears gentle around climax: he made it up

indicators.note: around puts the word for gentle on either side of the word for climax

parts.note: gentle means soft
a climax is a peak

indicators.note: in a down clue, up means the word for made it is read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: to have made it through is to have survived, or lived

explanation.surface: A puzzling account of a man who shows up at a gentle climax, and who invented the whole thing.
explanation.walkthrough: S(PEAK)OFT, then HE as written, then LIVED reversed to give DEVIL. The definition is a description of when the phrase is said.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom is said when someone being talked about turns up at that very moment.

clue.text: Eliot, Eliot & Eliot

parts.note: the poet Eliot is T. S. Eliot, so three Eliots show his initials three times over; it also reads as three siblings sharing one name

explanation.surface: A roll-call of three people all named Eliot.
explanation.walkthrough: The poet T. S. Eliot gives the initials TS; three of him are a triple TS. Three children all called Eliot would also be born together.
explanation.definitionFit: Three identical-looking siblings born at one birth share a name here, so the trio is a set of multiple-birth children.

clue.text: Gone sinister

definitions.meaning: having departed or gone away, as someone who has quit a room
in heraldry and Latin, sinister means on the port or non-dexter side

explanation.surface: Something has turned dark and vanished.
explanation.definitionFit: Departed is a past participle synonym; sinister is the Latin and heraldic word for the port-hand side.

clue.text: See you when you arrive, but not first off

indicators.note: off means the remaining letters go wrong and are rearranged
not first means the opening letter of the phrase you arrive is dropped

explanation.surface: A farewell timed for when the other person turns up, minus the first moment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not first' removes Y from YOU ARRIVE, leaving OUARRIVE, which 'off' rearranges into the French phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase for goodbye literally means until we meet again, the same idea as the casual parting words.

clue.text: See 10
Had an impact on camp

definitions.meaning: to have influenced or moved something
camp as an adjective means showy, mannered and theatrical

explanation.surface: Something made a difference to a campsite.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb sense is influenced; the adjective sense is pretentious or artificial in manner, a synonym of camp.

clue.text: Shops here are holding scoundrel

indicators.note: holding means the word are wraps around the word for scoundrel

parts.note: a cad is a dishonourable man, a scoundrel

explanation.surface: A warning that the local shops are harbouring a villain.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered passage lined with stores is where you would find shops, so the definition describes the place.

clue.text: Still confused about a copy of the Iliad?

definitions.text: Still confused about a copy of the Iliad?

indicators.note: about means the jumbled letters go around the letter a
confused means the letters of the word Still are jumbled

parts.note: the Iliad is Homer's epic in ancient Greek, so a copy is a Greek tome, a big book

explanation.surface: Someone holding a copy of Homer's Iliad admits they still cannot make sense of it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'confused' rearranges STILL into ITSLL, 'about' places A inside to make ITSALL, then a copy of the Iliad is a GREEK TOME. The whole clue also describes the phrase's meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: The saying means something is beyond understanding, exactly how a reader without ancient Greek feels before Homer's original text.

clue.text: Hector is by definition adorable

parts.note: the Latin per se means in itself, intrinsically, by definition
adorable means cute

explanation.surface: A boast that someone named Hector is inherently lovely.
explanation.walkthrough: Hector looks like the Trojan hero's name, but here it is the verb to hector, to bully.
explanation.definitionFit: To hector is to bully and harass, the same as hounding someone relentlessly.

clue.text: Tree surgeon's plant is about right for me

parts.note: a fir is a type of tree

indicators.note: about here means the letters are moved around, rearranged

explanation.surface: A tree surgeon's sapling is sorted out properly for the speaker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' rearranges SURGEONS, PLANT IS and R together into the last two words, after FIR.
explanation.definitionFit: The pronoun 'me' belongs to the grammatical category used for the speaker alone, as opposed to 'us' or 'you'.

clue.text: In retreat to meet up: majority of one, missing a member

indicators.note: retreat means the hidden letters run backwards
In means the letters sit inside the run of words meet up: majority

explanation.surface: A reluctant plan to meet, with most people agreeing while one is absent.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' hides EETUPMA in 'meet up: majority' and 'retreat' turns it around. 'majority of one' looks like the parliamentary phrase but is a split.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who has lost a limb is someone missing a member, member meaning an arm or leg.

clue.text: Got together in hospital with a composer

indicators.note: in places the word for got together inside the word for hospital

parts.note: SAN is short for sanatorium, a hospital
got together means met

explanation.surface: Two people met in hospital alongside a composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Bedřich Smetana was a Czech composer, best known for Má vlast and The Bartered Bride.

clue.text: Exploit dispute minister rejected in agreement

indicators.note: in places the turned letters inside the word for agreement

parts.note: OK signals agreement, as in giving the OK

indicators.note: rejected means the joined words are turned back to front

parts.note: a row is a dispute or quarrel
REV, short for Reverend, is a minister of the church

explanation.surface: A quarrel in which a minister is turned down despite having seemed to agree.
explanation.definitionFit: To exploit staff is to make them toil to excess, so the verb means driving people too hard.

clue.text: Shabby at interrupting dog instructions

indicators.note: interrupting means the word at breaks into the middle of the commands

parts.note: down and heel are two commands given to a dog

explanation.surface: A shabby dog-trainer is cut short while giving commands.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes someone looking poor and run-down, like a worn-out shoe, which matches shabby.

clue.text: More delectable than a salmon terrine is egg roll for starters

indicators.note: for starters means the opening letter of each word from than to roll is taken

explanation.surface: A menu verdict: an egg roll beats salmon terrine as a first course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'for starters' takes the first letters of 'than a salmon terrine is egg roll'. Starters also fits the menu picture.
explanation.definitionFit: Comparative of a word for flavoursome, so it means having a better flavour, as more delectable does.

clue.text: Half in the dark and troubled in my disgrace

indicators.note: Half means only the first half of the word for in the dark is used

parts.note: to be in the dark is to be ignorant

indicators.note: troubled means the letters of in my are stirred up and rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone half kept in the dark and troubled by their own shame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Half' takes IGNO from IGNORANT; 'troubled' rearranges IN MY into MINY.
explanation.definitionFit: Ignominy is public shame or dishonour, a synonym of disgrace.

clue.text: Actual consumer suffers with a twist in the tail

indicators.text: with a twist in the tail
indicators.note: a twist in the tail means only the final stretch of the word for suffers is turned around

parts.note: to suffer something is to endure it, so suffers means endures

explanation.surface: A shopper who suffers from a nasty surprise at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with a twist in the tail' reverses only the last three letters of ENDURES, turning RES into SER.
explanation.definitionFit: The final buyer or operator who uses a product, as opposed to a reseller, is the actual consumer.

clue.text: Hears endless adverts? Not with these!

definitions.text: Hears endless adverts? Not with these!

indicators.note: endless means the first and last letters of Hears are removed

parts.note: a plug is a piece of publicity, an advert

explanation.surface: Someone tired of hearing endless adverts is told they will not with these in.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' strips Hears to EAR; adverts are PLUGS. The whole clue also describes what the answer stops.
explanation.definitionFit: Foam stoppers worn in the ears block sound, so with them in you hear no adverts.

clue.text: See 10
Planning a set dinner to finish badly

indicators.note: planning means the letters are arranged afresh, laid out in a new order

explanation.surface: Organising a fixed-menu dinner that ends in disaster.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes something that ends unhappily, with someone crying, so it means a bad conclusion.

clue.text: Conclude being educated not at fault

indicators.note: fault means the remaining letters are flawed and rearranged
not means the word at is removed from educated

explanation.surface: Deciding that an educated person cannot be to blame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' removes AT from EDUCATED, leaving EDUCED, and 'fault' rearranges that.
explanation.definitionFit: To infer a result by reasoning is to reach a conclusion, so the verb is a synonym of conclude.

clue.text: Thrill from sexy act with her unclothed

indicators.note: unclothed strips the outer letters, the covering, from each of the words sexy, act, with and her

explanation.surface: A racy scene of an undressed woman performing a provocative act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unclothed' removes the outer letters of each word: sEXy, aCt, wITh, hEr.
explanation.definitionFit: To thrill someone is to stir them up with excitement, so the verbs are synonyms.

clue.text: Formerly one in a hundred? On the contrary

indicators.note: in on its own would put one inside the word for a hundred
on the contrary flips that, so the letter for a hundred goes inside one instead

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred

explanation.surface: Musing on whether something used to be a one-in-a-hundred event.
explanation.walkthrough: 'one in a hundred' would put ONE inside C; 'On the contrary' reverses the roles, putting C inside ONE.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means at some earlier time, a synonym of formerly.

clue.text: Object to experimental mice being present locally

parts.note: an end is an object or aim

indicators.note: experimental means the letters of mice are tried out in a new order

explanation.surface: An objection to mice being used in laboratory experiments.
explanation.walkthrough: Object looks like a verb, to protest, but it is the noun meaning aim.
explanation.definitionFit: A disease or species found regularly in one region is native to that area, so it is present locally.

clue.text: What to wear in case?

parts.note: reads as packing advice for a suitcase or emergency, but a case is a court action and a suit is clothing

explanation.surface: Packing advice about which outfit to bring just in case.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue splits the answer into a law suit, the outfit for a legal case.
explanation.definitionFit: A legal action brought in court is a case, and a suit is also something worn.

clue.text: See 13
Preserved member of an ancient civilisation

definitions.meaning: food that is preserved is stored in a tin, read as two words
belonging to the Andean empire conquered by the Spanish in the sixteenth century

explanation.surface: A mummified figure from an ancient culture.
explanation.definitionFit: Tinned food is preserved; the adjective also names a person of the Peruvian empire ruled from Cuzco.

clue.text: It's King Lear BBC can blame for losing odd characters treatment

indicators.note: losing odd characters means dropping the first, third and other odd-placed letters of each word, keeping the even ones

explanation.surface: A complaint that the BBC's production of King Lear is to blame for something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'losing odd characters' keeps the even letters of each word: iTs, kInG, lEaR, bBc, cAn, bLaMe.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a branded herbal ointment rubbed on aches and pains, a remedy or treatment.
